candidates.title: Commission and lock a compact industrial robot-axis shock absorber
candidates.objective: With the representative axis isolated, physically loosen the adjuster setscrew, rotate the numbered collar on an ECO OEM .35M-form damper, retighten the setscrew, operate a guarded physical cycle control, and iteratively obtain two repeatable carriage stops without bottoming, overload, excessive rebound, or setting drift.
skills: hex-key alignment and insertion into a recessed setscrew
collar grasping and controlled fine rotation
bimanual stabilization while loosening and locking
iterative adjustment from observed dynamic response
physical control actuation and guarded inspection
candidates.success_conditions: Use a rigid PhysX carriage whose motor, contacts, spring return, damper stroke, and hard stop are physically simulated. Test energy must be at least 0.85 J, corresponding to 5% of the published 17.0 Nm/cycle maximum, with impact velocity inside the published 0.3–3.30 m/s range. The robot must physically loosen the setscrew before turning the collar and physically relock it afterward. Success requires two consecutive cycles with no piston travel beyond 12.0 mm, no hard-stop strike, no excessive rebound, no overload, and collar drift below a declared measured tolerance during a post-lock witness-torque test. Award partial credit for successful key engagement, unlocking, adjustment, and locking. Zero score for adjustment while the axis is energized, direct pose/velocity/damping writes, collision suppression, hidden stage flags, damaged threads, dropped tools, or a hard-stop impact.
candidates.industrial_value: The AZ-100 service manual establishes shock-absorber adjustment as robot-axis maintenance, while the Enidine catalog establishes a real compact adjustable damper, its operating envelope, internal adjustment mechanism, and setscrew retention. This makes the task relevant to commissioning and maintaining automation equipment that supports scalable robot and compute-infrastructure production, without claiming that the Enidine model is interchangeable with the AZ-100 component.
candidates.dexterity: High but feasible: the robot must align and seat a hex key, counterhold a small cylindrical body, unlock a retained collar, make fine rotations, reinsert or maintain tool engagement, apply bounded locking torque, and judge the result from repeated physical impacts rather than collar angle alone.

candidates.asset_plan: Author a full-scale representative fixture around the published ECO OEM .35M envelope: 12.0 mm stroke, M16×1.5 body, 100.6 mm body length, 11.2 mm rod diameter, 14.5 mm adjustment diameter, and published force/energy/velocity limits. Preserve a physical 180-degree collar and a contact-bearing setscrew; disclose the independently chosen setscrew size, friction, thread torque, damping interpolation, and carriage parameters as modeling assumptions rather than manufacturer calibration. Start with an 8 kg guarded carriage at 0.5 m/s (1.0 J), then validate energy balance, 12 mm travel, hard-stop contact, rebound, low/high-adjustment controls, lock holding, parameter sensitivity, and reset repeatability before connecting YAM. The cycle control must be physically pressed by the robot, and no task object may be teleported or welded during execution.
candidates.risk: The catalog does not publish collar torque, setscrew dimensions, friction, or a complete force-versus-setting curve. These are nonessential calibration details rather than an unknown retention mechanism: model them as bounded assumptions and require component-level sensitivity and witness-torque tests before any full demo. The small interface may require an enlarged but mechanically equivalent robot-accessible key head; any enlargement must be disclosed and must preserve the collar/setscrew operation.

candidates.title: Replace and rebalance a spring-balancer-supported industrial tool
candidates.objective: Lock and proof-check an EWA-15 drum, support and exchange its suspended tool, adjust spring preload through the worm while observing the gauge, and release the lock under control until the replacement remains balanced.
candidates.success_conditions: The pin must physically enter a drum slot and resist an upward/downward proof motion before removal. The 9–15 kg replacement must be attached and supported before unlock, then remain hands-off without abrupt rise, drop, or overtravel. Zero score for unlocked removal, unloaded release, snap-back, tool drop, direct state writes, teleportation, or welded retention.
candidates.industrial_value: The manufacturer explicitly prescribes drum locking, load support, preload adjustment, attachment before release, and final balance checking during suspended-tool replacement.
candidates.dexterity: High: indexed locking, proof loading, heavy-load stabilization, hook manipulation, wrench engagement, gauge feedback, and guarded release must be coordinated.

candidates.asset_plan: A representative fixture needs a six-position physical drum lock, pull/turn pin, worm-driven preload, readable gauge, latching hook, 1.3 m payout constraint, and 9–15 kg load. Validate false seating, lock holding, payout, preload direction, hands-off balance, snap-back behavior, overload, and reset repeatability before robot integration.
candidates.risk: The procedure and specification row are now cited from the source that actually contains them, correcting the prior source mismatch. Essential lock, worm, gauge, hook, and spring geometry remains undimensioned, and the pinned YAM payload capability is unverified.
missing_evidence: Dimensioned lock-pin, drum-slot, worm, gauge, hook, and housing geometry
Defensible worm ratio and spring torque-versus-payout bounds
Pinned-YAM reach, grip-force, and payload validation for a 9–15 kg suspended load

candidates.title: Track and tension an industrial robot timing belt
candidates.objective: With power isolated, adjust the two-sided tracking mechanism in small increments, manually traverse the axis, observe lateral belt travel, and iteratively center the belt without slack or over-tension.
candidates.success_conditions: The robot must physically operate both adjusters and manually traverse the axis after each correction. Success requires centered tracking over repeated full traversals and a sourced model-specific tension criterion. Zero score for powered adjustment, direct belt-state writes, invisible centering constraints, flange climbing, slack, over-tension, or damage.
candidates.industrial_value: The robot manufacturer identifies tracking and tensioning as required maintenance and warns that incorrect adjustment reduces performance or causes premature belt failure.
candidates.dexterity: Potentially high because paired fine adjustment, manual traversal, and diagnosis of belt creep must be alternated, but the essential manipulation depends on credible deformable belt contact.

candidates.asset_plan: Do not implement without a validated Isaac Sim 6.1 belt/contact example. A faithful fixture needs sourced pulley, flange, belt-profile, span, adjuster, and carriage geometry plus tests for lateral tracking, flange climbing, slack, over-tension, manual traversal, and repeatability.
candidates.risk: This is a deformable closed-loop belt problem, and the acquired inputs contain neither a validated compatible solver example nor sufficient model-specific geometry and tension data.
missing_evidence: Validated belt/contact example compatible with the pinned Isaac Sim 6.1 Arena/YAM runtime
Dimensioned belt, pulley, flange, span, adjuster, and carriage geometry
Model-specific numeric tension or deflection criterion
Physics validation that asymmetric tension creates credible lateral tracking

selection_reason: The ECO OEM .35M commissioning task is the only candidate with primary evidence for industrial robot relevance, essential adjustment and retention mechanics, full-scale body geometry, stroke, velocity range, energy limit, return/propelling data, and a plausible rigid-PhysX implementation in the pinned Isaac Sim 6.1/YAM runtime. Its collar-unlock-adjust-relock workflow and dynamically verified stopping objective are materially different from connector insertion, module exchange, static clearance adjustment, generic knob rotation, and the supplied benchmark task families. Review of the acquired six-suite records and existing novelty artifacts found no objective combining physical damper setting retention with measured impact-energy commissioning. The remaining unpublished coefficients can be bounded modeling assumptions tested before robot integration; no essential contact or retention mechanism is unknown.
